In this timeline, the great empires never outlived the oath,
  and the plowland became the first constitution of the world,
    and kings were crowned landlords of the whole map,
      and cities grew within walled fiefs, each with its own toll, court, and coin,
        and the printing press spread not freedom but charters of fealty,
          so every newspaper began by naming the lord of the press,
            and the industrial age rose not by breaking the chain but by leasing it,
              with factories as manors, workers as serfs of the steam engine,
                and wages as rents paid to the owners of the piston,
                  while the airships of the great houses drifted over the fields,
                    and the satellites of later centuries still asked for tribute,
                      and the world, even in the age of code, remained a living hierarchy of homage,
                        where the future itself was held in fief by those who could swear the old oaths.
